newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-"WEIRD" DEFEAT FOR EX-CHAMPION COURIER.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-"WEIRD" DEFEAT FOR EX-CHAMPION COURIER.

text.p: Former champion Jim Courier bowed out of the French Open at the first hurdle on Tuesday, victim of what he described as the "weirdest" defeat of his career.

Courier, who won consecutive titles at Roland Garros in 1991 and 1992 and was a finalist in 1993, lost in five sets to Sweden's Magnus Larsson in a wildly fluctuating contest which had appeared to be heading the American's way.
Despite trailing by two sets and 4-2, he looked to have salvaged his reputation as Larsson suddenly found himself unable to keep the ball in the court and allowed him back to two sets all.
But the script then went drastically wrong from Courier's point of view as Larsson pulled himself together to win 6-1 6-2 4-6 1-6 6-4, leaving the former world number one to ponder a few home truths.

"It was a surprise how pathetic I was out there," admitted Courier, whose previous earliest exit at Roland Garros had been the fourth round. "I had a good week of preparation but today I felt like an alien. I felt out of my skin as if I was jetlagged. There's no logical explanation for me to play that pathetic.

"I've been in some pretty weird matches but that was as weird as they come. He couldn't hit the ball in the court at times, but the disappointing fact for me is the way I played not the actual outcome. It's pretty sad actually.
"It was a bad match, but the sun's going to rise tomorrow and I'll be on a plane following it."
Now ranked 20th in the world, Courier was unseeded this time but his departure is a bonus for those in the bottom half of the draw.

Most of the seeded names still remain but Britain's Tim Henman, seeded 14th on the strength of his form earlier in the year prior to an elbow injury, is still waiting to record his first victory on Parisian clay.

Henman did his best to fight back against France's Olivier Delaitre but eventually lost 6-2 2-6 1-6 6-2 6-4 which at least gives himself plenty of extra preparation time on grass before next month's Wimbledon.
Seventh seed Marcelo Rios from Chile, one of the dark horses in the men's draw, was also forced to five sets but survived to beat Wayne Black of Zimbabwe 6-4 5-7 4-6 6-2 6-1.
It was a similar story for ninth seed Carlos Moya whose unfinished match against fellow Spaniard Alberto Martin, level at two sets all overnight, was settled in 37 minutes on another sunny day.
Moya won the decisive set 6-3, the crucial break arriving in the sixth game when Martin saved five break points only to hit a forehand long to concede the sixth.
In the women's singles, Martina Hingis and Steffi Graf moved imperiously into the second round after one-sided contests.

Hingis, the 16-year-old top seed, dismissed Slovakia's Henrieta Nagyova 6-0 6-2 while Graf maintained her remarkable first round record at Roland Garros with a 6-1 6-4 victory over Argentine Paola Suarez.
It was Graf's 15th successive first round win in Paris without dropping a set, dating all the way back to 1983 when she recorded her first Grand Slam singles victory at the tender age of 13.

Only France's Mary Pierce has managed to beat Graf on Parisian clay since her dramatic final defeat to Monica Seles in 1992 but the German dismissed locker-room wisdom that she is more vulnerable than usual this year.
"I felt very good out there and I served a lot stronger than in Strasbourg last week," said Graf. "Until the last few games I didn't really make too many mistakes."
None of the other women's seeds in action during the first half of the day dropped a set.
